planting.note: Direct sow in fall so seed overwinters outdoors, or collect seed and give 60 days of cold-moist stratification in the refrigerator before a spring sowing; established clumps are also easily divided in early spring.

directions: This Southern and Central Appalachian endemic grows naturally on thin, rocky soils near granitic outcrops from West Virginia south to northern Georgia, and it tolerates leaner, drier ground better than most of its mountain mint relatives. Plant in full sun to light shade and avoid heavy, wet clay, since good drainage is more important to this species than fertility. The dense, rounded clusters of tiny white flowers open later in summer than many other mountain mints and are relentlessly visited by wasps, small native bees, and a wide range of butterflies and skipper species. Once sited well it spreads slowly by rhizome to form a durable, aromatic patch that rarely needs division.

planting.note: Sow outdoors in fall for natural cold-moist stratification, or hold seed in a moist medium in the refrigerator for 60-90 days before sowing in spring; tolerates dry, rocky soil so avoid overwatering after establishment.

directions: Native from Illinois and Virginia south to northern Florida, Loomis's mountain mint favors dry, sandy, or rocky woodland edges and forest borders rather than moist prairie ground, making it a good fit for lean, well-drained garden beds. Its silvery upper leaves and peppermint-scented foliage surround small pink-lavender flower clusters that open in mid to late summer. Like its relatives it is an outstanding nectar source, drawing large numbers of native bees, wasps, and butterflies over a long bloom period. Give it full sun and allow it room to spread gradually by rhizome, since crowded plantings reduce air flow and can invite mildew in humid climates.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into consistently moist soil, or cold-moist stratify seed for 3-8 weeks in the refrigerator before a spring sowing; keep soil damp through germination since this species comes from wet meadow and flatwoods habitat.

directions: Awned mountain mint is a coastal plain specialist found in damp flatwoods, wet meadow margins, and clearings from New Jersey south to Florida and west to Mississippi, and unlike most mountain mints it wants consistently moist to seasonally wet soil rather than dry, lean ground. It stays smaller and more compact than many congeners, forming clumps of narrow, aromatic leaves topped by tight white to pale lavender flower heads in mid to late summer. The abundant small flowers are a magnet for short-tongued native bees, wasps, and a variety of butterflies looking for accessible nectar. Site it at the edge of a rain garden, pond margin, or low meadow spot where it will not dry out during the growing season.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Sow in fall directly into moist soil to satisfy natural cold-moist stratification, or refrigerate moistened seed for 4-8 weeks before spring sowing; keep the seedbed consistently damp, mimicking the wet pine flatwoods this species calls home.

directions: This smooth-stemmed mountain mint is a true Deep South endemic, restricted to wet pine flatwoods and seasonally saturated soils from southeastern South Carolina through peninsular and Panhandle Florida into southeastern Alabama. Unlike the majority of mountain mints, it needs soil that stays reliably moist and is best suited to a wet meadow, pond edge, or low spot that mimics natural flatwoods hydrology. Its whitish, tightly clustered summer flowers are a strong draw for small native bees, wasps, and butterflies, and the plant fills a pollinator niche in wetland gardens that most drought-tolerant mountain mints cannot occupy. Because its natural range is narrow, gardeners outside the Deep South coastal plain should confirm sourcing to avoid confusion with the more common P. muticum or P. floridanum.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Direct sow outdoors in fall so seed experiences a full winter of cold-moist stratification, since like other Silphium species it germinates poorly without it; if sowing in spring, cold-stratify seed in moist sand in the refrigerator for 60-90 days first. Plants form a deep taproot and resent transplanting once established.

directions: A little-grown Southern Appalachian rosinweed native to open woods, glades, and roadside banks of North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, and Tennessee, this species is easily overlooked next to its better-known cousins prairie dock and compass plant. It sends up a stout, upright clump of coarse, toothed leaves that by midsummer is topped with bright yellow daisy-like flower heads well above the foliage. Like other silphiums it develops a long taproot that makes it extremely drought tolerant once established and best sown or planted in its permanent spot. The flowers are heavily visited by native bees and butterflies, and the seed heads that follow are a favored late-season food source for goldfinches and other seed-eating birds.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)
